column2: Morgen heb ik een afspraak.
column3: Tomorrow I have an appointment.
column4: You have an appointment tomorrow. Say so about yourself, starting with Morgen.
column5: Morgen is the first constituent, so the finite verb heb comes second and ik follows. Do not say Morgen ik heb.

column2: Om negen uur begint de vergadering.
column3: The meeting starts at nine o'clock.
column4: The meeting starts at nine. Tell a colleague, starting with Om negen uur.
column5: Om negen uur is one time phrase, so it counts as one constituent. Begint is second; the subject de vergadering comes after it.

column2: Gisteren heeft hij de brief gestuurd.
column3: Yesterday he sent the letter.
column4: A colleague asks about the letter. Say that he sent it yesterday, starting with Gisteren.
column5: Gisteren takes first position, so heeft is second and the subject hij follows. The participle gestuurd stays at the end.

column2: Hier kun je parkeren.
column3: You can park here.
column4: A visitor asks where to park. Point to the spot and start with Hier.
column5: Hier is the first constituent, so the finite verb kun is second. The infinitive parkeren closes the sentence.

column2: Na het werk ga ik naar de sportschool.
column3: After work I go to the gym.
column4: Describe your evening plan, starting with Na het werk. Speak about yourself.
column5: Na het werk is one phrase in first position. Ga is second and ik follows it.

column2: Vandaag moeten we eerder weg.
column3: Today we have to leave earlier.
column4: Your team has to leave early today. Say it, starting with Vandaag.
column5: Vandaag is first, moeten is second and we follows. The particle weg stays at the end of the clause.

column2: In de zomer gaan wij naar Spanje.
column3: In the summer we go to Spain.
column4: Tell a friend your holiday plan, starting with In de zomer.
column5: In de zomer is one constituent, so gaan is second and wij follows it.

column2: Soms neemt zij de fiets.
column3: Sometimes she takes the bike.
column4: Explain how a colleague sometimes travels. Start with Soms.
column5: Soms is a one-word first constituent. The finite verb neemt is second; zij follows.

column2: Daarna drinken we koffie.
column3: Afterwards we drink coffee.
column4: Describe what happens after the meal. Start with Daarna.
column5: Daarna is first, so the verb drinken comes second and the subject we follows.

column2: Op maandag werkt hij thuis.
column3: On Mondays he works from home.
column4: Explain a colleague's routine, starting with Op maandag.
column5: Op maandag is one phrase in first position. Werkt is second and hij follows it.

column2: Volgende week komt mijn zus op bezoek.
column3: Next week my sister is coming to visit.
column4: Tell a friend about a visit. Start with Volgende week.
column5: Volgende week is one time constituent. Komt is second; the subject mijn zus follows. Op bezoek stays at the end.

column2: Om zes uur eten wij samen.
column3: At six o'clock we eat together.
column4: Tell your family when dinner is. Start with Om zes uur.
column5: Om zes uur is one phrase, so eten is second and wij follows.

column2: Thuis lees ik graag.
column3: At home I like to read.
column4: Say where you like to read. Start with Thuis.
column5: Thuis is the first constituent, so lees is second and ik follows. Graag stays after the subject.

column2: Binnenkort verhuizen mijn buren.
column3: Soon my neighbours are moving.
column4: Share news about the neighbours, starting with Binnenkort.
column5: Binnenkort is first, so the verb verhuizen is second and the subject mijn buren follows it.

column2: Ik blijf thuis omdat ik ziek ben.
column3: I am staying at home because I am ill.
column4: Explain why you stay at home today. Use omdat.
column5: After omdat the finite verb moves to the end of its clause: omdat ik ziek ben, not omdat ik ben ziek.

column2: Zij komt later omdat de trein vertraging heeft.
column3: She is coming later because the train is delayed.
column4: A colleague is late. Explain the reason with omdat.
column5: In the omdat clause the verb heeft goes to the end, after vertraging.

column2: We nemen de bus omdat het regent.
column3: We take the bus because it is raining.
column4: Explain why you are not cycling. Use omdat.
column5: Het regent is a short clause, and the verb regent is last: omdat het regent.

column2: Hij leert Nederlands omdat hij hier werkt.
column3: He is learning Dutch because he works here.
column4: Explain why a colleague learns Dutch. Use omdat.
column5: The omdat clause ends with the verb werkt, after hier.

column2: Ik bel je omdat ik een vraag heb.
column3: I am calling you because I have a question.
column4: Start a phone call by giving your reason. Use omdat.
column5: The verb heb is at the end of the clause: omdat ik een vraag heb.

column2: Ze is moe omdat ze vannacht weinig heeft geslapen.
column3: She is tired because she slept little last night.
column4: Explain why a friend looks tired. Use omdat.
column5: With two verbs the finite verb heeft comes before the participle geslapen, and both close the clause.

column2: Wij zijn vroeg vertrokken omdat het druk was.
column3: We left early because it was busy.
column4: Explain why you left early. Use omdat.
column5: Was is the last word of the omdat clause.

column2: Ik neem een paraplu mee omdat het gaat regenen.
column3: I am taking an umbrella because it is going to rain.
column4: Explain why you take an umbrella. Use omdat.
column5: Gaat regenen is a verb group at the end: first the finite verb gaat, then the infinitive regenen.

column2: De winkel is dicht omdat het feestdag is.
column3: The shop is closed because it is a public holiday.
column4: Explain to a tourist why the shop is closed. Use omdat.
column5: The finite verb is closes the clause: omdat het feestdag is.

column2: Hij kan niet komen omdat hij moet werken.
column3: He cannot come because he has to work.
column4: Explain why a friend cannot come. Use omdat.
column5: The verb group moet werken ends the clause, with the finite verb moet first.

column2: Ik ruim op omdat er bezoek komt.
column3: I am tidying up because visitors are coming.
column4: Explain why you are cleaning. Use omdat.
column5: Komt is last. Er bezoek komt keeps the verb at the end of the omdat clause.

column2: Mijn collega belt omdat de printer niet werkt.
column3: My colleague is calling because the printer is not working.
column4: Explain why your colleague phones. Use omdat.
column5: Niet comes before the verb at the end: omdat de printer niet werkt.

column2: We wachten omdat de dokter nog bezig is.
column3: We are waiting because the doctor is still busy.
column4: Explain to a friend why you are still waiting. Use omdat.
column5: The finite verb is closes the omdat clause, after bezig.

column2: Zij fietst omdat ze de bus heeft gemist.
column3: She is cycling because she missed the bus.
column4: Explain why a colleague cycles today. Use omdat.
column5: The verb group heeft gemist ends the clause: omdat ze de bus heeft gemist.

column2: Ik denk dat het morgen mooi weer is.
column3: I think the weather will be nice tomorrow.
column4: Share your opinion about tomorrow's weather. Start with Ik denk dat.
column5: After dat the finite verb goes to the end: dat het morgen mooi weer is.

column2: Hij zegt dat hij later komt.
column3: He says that he is coming later.
column4: Report a colleague's message. Start with Hij zegt dat.
column5: In the dat clause the verb komt is last.

column2: Ik weet dat jij hard werkt.
column3: I know that you work hard.
column4: Compliment a colleague. Start with Ik weet dat.
column5: Werkt closes the dat clause, after hard.

column2: Zij vertelt dat de les is uitgevallen.
column3: She tells us that the lesson has been cancelled.
column4: Pass on news about a cancelled lesson. Start with Zij vertelt dat.
column5: The verb group is uitgevallen is at the end: first the auxiliary is, then the participle uitgevallen.

column2: We hopen dat de trein op tijd rijdt.
column3: We hope that the train runs on time.
column4: Say what you hope about the train. Start with We hopen dat.
column5: Rijdt is the last word of the dat clause.

column2: Ik geloof dat dit de juiste weg is.
column3: I believe this is the right way.
column4: Give your view while lost. Start with Ik geloof dat.
column5: The finite verb is closes the dat clause.

column2: Jij zegt dat je geen tijd hebt.
column3: You say that you have no time.
column4: Repeat what a friend told you. Start with Jij zegt dat.
column5: Hebt goes to the end of the clause, after geen tijd.

column2: Ik hoor dat het restaurant open is.
column3: I hear that the restaurant is open.
column4: Share what you heard about a restaurant. Start with Ik hoor dat.
column5: Open is, with the finite verb is last.

column2: Hij merkt dat zijn telefoon leeg is.
column3: He notices that his phone is empty.
column4: Describe a colleague realising his battery is dead. Start with Hij merkt dat.
column5: Leeg is: the finite verb is closes the clause.

column2: Ik vind dat dit een goed idee is.
column3: I think this is a good idea.
column4: Give your opinion on a plan. Start with Ik vind dat.
column5: Een goed idee is, with the verb is at the end of the dat clause.

column2: Zij weet dat de afspraak om drie uur begint.
column3: She knows that the appointment starts at three.
column4: Say what a colleague knows about the appointment. Start with Zij weet dat.
column5: Begint is the last word of the dat clause, after the time phrase.

column2: Wij zien dat het licht uit is.
column3: We see that the light is off.
column4: Describe what you notice when you arrive. Start with Wij zien dat.
column5: Uit is: the verb is is last, after uit.

column2: Ik begrijp dat je moe bent.
column3: I understand that you are tired.
column4: Show understanding to a friend. Start with Ik begrijp dat.
column5: Bent closes the dat clause: dat je moe bent.

column2: Zeg tegen haar dat ik zo kom.
column3: Tell her that I am coming soon.
column4: Ask a colleague to pass on a message. Start with Zeg tegen haar dat.
column5: The imperative Zeg is a main clause; the dat clause ends with the verb kom.

column2: Als het regent, blijf ik thuis.
column3: If it rains, I stay at home.
column4: Say what you do on rainy days. Start with Als.
column5: The als clause comes first, so the main clause starts with its verb: blijf ik, not ik blijf.

column2: Ik bel je als ik thuis ben.
column3: I will call you when I am home.
column4: Promise a friend a call. Use als.
column5: When the als clause follows, its verb goes to the end: als ik thuis ben.

column2: Als je moe bent, moet je rusten.
column3: If you are tired, you have to rest.
column4: Give advice to a tired friend. Start with Als.
column5: Bent closes the als clause. The main clause then begins with moet, followed by je.

column2: Als de bus komt, stappen we in.
column3: When the bus comes, we get on.
column4: Tell your group what to do. Start with Als.
column5: Komt is last in the als clause, so stappen comes first in the main clause.

column2: Hij helpt altijd als ik hem nodig heb.
column3: He always helps when I need him.
column4: Praise a helpful colleague. Use als.
column5: The als clause ends with the verb heb.

column2: Als ik tijd heb, lees ik een boek.
column3: When I have time, I read a book.
column4: Describe your habit with free time. Start with Als.
column5: After the als clause the main verb lees comes first, then ik.

column2: Zij neemt een taxi als het laat is.
column3: She takes a taxi when it is late.
column4: Explain how a friend gets home late. Use als.
column5: Als here means when, for a repeated situation. The verb is closes the clause.

column2: Als het koud is, draag ik een jas.
column3: When it is cold, I wear a coat.
column4: Say what you wear in cold weather. Start with Als.
column5: After the als clause the main verb draag precedes ik.

column2: Als je vragen hebt, kun je me bellen.
column3: If you have questions, you can call me.
column4: Invite a colleague to ask for help. Start with Als.
column5: Hebt ends the als clause, and kun je follows as the main clause.

column2: We gaan wandelen als de zon schijnt.
column3: We go for a walk if the sun shines.
column4: Make a plan that depends on the weather. Use als.
column5: Schijnt is last in the als clause.

column2: Als hij komt, zeg ik het hem.
column3: If he comes, I will tell him.
column4: Promise to pass on information. Start with Als.
column5: Komt closes the als clause; zeg ik follows.

column2: Als ik honger heb, eet ik een boterham.
column3: When I am hungry, I eat a sandwich.
column4: Describe what you do when you are hungry. Start with Als.
column5: The als clause ends with heb; eet ik then starts the main clause.

column2: Als de winkel dicht is, gaan wij naar huis.
column3: If the shop is closed, we go home.
column4: Tell your group the plan. Start with Als.
column5: Is closes the als clause; gaan wij follows.

column2: Als je de weg niet weet, vraag het aan iemand.
column3: If you do not know the way, ask someone.
column4: Give a tourist advice. Start with Als.
column5: Weet is last in the als clause. The main clause is an instruction, so it starts with vraag.

column2: Ik wacht tot de bus komt.
column3: I wait until the bus comes.
column4: Say what you are waiting for. Use tot.
column5: Tot introduces an end point, and the verb komt goes to the end of its clause.

column2: Zij werkt tot het donker wordt.
column3: She works until it gets dark.
column4: Describe a colleague who works late. Use tot.
column5: Wordt is last in the tot clause.

column2: We blijven hier tot jij klaar bent.
column3: We are staying here until you are ready.
column4: Tell a friend you will wait. Use tot.
column5: Bent ends the clause after klaar.

column2: Hij slaapt tot de wekker gaat.
column3: He sleeps until the alarm goes off.
column4: Describe a heavy sleeper. Use tot.
column5: Gaat closes the tot clause.

column2: Wacht even tot ik terugbel.
column3: Wait a moment until I call back.
column4: Ask a colleague to wait. Use tot.
column5: Terugbel is a separable verb, written as one word at the end of a subordinate clause.

column2: Ik oefen tot ik het kan.
column3: I practise until I can do it.
column4: Describe your approach to learning. Use tot.
column5: Kan is the last word of the tot clause.

column2: Zij zoekt tot ze haar sleutels vindt.
column3: She searches until she finds her keys.
column4: Describe a friend searching for keys. Use tot.
column5: Vindt is last, after haar sleutels.

column2: We lopen door tot we het park zien.
column3: We keep walking until we see the park.
column4: Give directions to a friend. Use tot.
column5: Zien closes the clause, after het park.

column2: Hij blijft rustig tot het voorbij is.
column3: He stays calm until it is over.
column4: Describe a calm colleague in a crisis. Use tot.
column5: Is closes the clause, after voorbij.

column2: Ik lees tot het tijd is om te slapen.
column3: I read until it is time to sleep.
column4: Describe your evening routine. Use tot.
column5: Is is last in the tot clause; om te slapen is a separate phrase inside it.

column2: Wij wachten tot de les begint.
column3: We wait until the lesson starts.
column4: Say what you are waiting for in the classroom. Use tot.
column5: Begint ends the tot clause.

column2: Blijf zitten tot de trein stilstaat.
column3: Stay seated until the train stops.
column4: Give an instruction on a train. Use tot.
column5: Stilstaat is one word at the end of the clause.

column2: Zij kookt tot de soep klaar is.
column3: She cooks until the soup is ready.
column4: Describe someone making soup. Use tot.
column5: Is closes the clause after klaar.

column2: Ik spaar tot ik genoeg geld heb.
column3: I save until I have enough money.
column4: Explain how you save for a purchase. Use tot.
column5: Heb is last, after genoeg geld.

column2: Toen ik wakker werd, regende het.
column3: When I woke up, it was raining.
column4: Tell what the weather was like when you woke up. Start with Toen.
column5: Toen refers to one moment in the past. The clause ends with werd, and the main clause then starts with the verb regende.

column2: Toen wij aankwamen, was het station vol.
column3: When we arrived, the station was full.
column4: Describe your arrival. Start with Toen.
column5: Aankwamen is last in the toen clause; the main clause starts with was.

column2: Hij belde mij toen ik aan het koken was.
column3: He phoned me when I was cooking.
column4: Say what you were doing when a friend phoned. Use toen.
column5: When the toen clause follows, its verb stays at the end: toen ik aan het koken was.

column2: Toen de les begon, zat iedereen op zijn plaats.
column3: When the lesson began, everyone was in their seat.
column4: Describe the start of a lesson. Start with Toen.
column5: Begon closes the toen clause, and zat comes first in the main clause.

column2: Ik zag haar toen ik de straat overstak.
column3: I saw her when I crossed the street.
column4: Tell about meeting someone in the street. Use toen.
column5: Oversteken is separable: in a toen clause its parts join, so overstak stands at the end.

column2: Toen het donker werd, gingen we naar huis.
column3: When it got dark, we went home.
column4: Tell what you did at nightfall. Start with Toen.
column5: Werd ends the toen clause; gingen we follows.

column2: Zij lachte toen ze het nieuws las.
column3: She laughed when she read the news.
column4: Describe a friend's reaction. Use toen.
column5: Las is last in the toen clause.

column2: Toen ik jong was, woonde ik in Gent.
column3: When I was young, I lived in Ghent.
column4: Talk about where you lived as a child. Start with Toen.
column5: Was ends the toen clause; woonde ik starts the main clause.

column2: Hij was moe toen hij thuiskwam.
column3: He was tired when he came home.
column4: Describe a colleague after work. Use toen.
column5: Thuiskwam is a single word at the end.

column2: Toen de trein vertrok, zwaaide ze.
column3: When the train left, she waved.
column4: Describe a farewell at the station. Start with Toen.
column5: Vertrok closes the toen clause; zwaaide comes first in the main clause.

column2: We aten net toen de telefoon ging.
column3: We were just eating when the phone rang.
column4: Tell what interrupted your meal. Use toen.
column5: Ging is last in the toen clause.

column2: Toen ik klein was, speelde ik buiten.
column3: When I was little, I played outside.
column4: Talk about your childhood. Start with Toen.
column5: Was ends the toen clause; speelde ik follows.

column2: Zij vergat haar tas toen ze uitstapte.
column3: She forgot her bag when she got off.
column4: Explain how a friend lost her bag. Use toen.
column5: Uitstapte is written as one word in the subordinate clause.

column2: Toen het begon te regenen, renden we naar binnen.
column3: When it began to rain, we ran inside.
column4: Tell what you did when the rain started. Start with Toen.
column5: Begon te regenen is the verb group ending the toen clause; renden we follows.

column2: Vorige week heb ik mijn tante gebeld.
column3: Last week I phoned my aunt.
column4: Tell a friend what you did last week. Use the perfect and start with Vorige week.
column5: Vorige week starts the sentence, so heb is second. The perfect uses heb plus the participle gebeld, which goes to the end.

column2: Ik werkte vroeger in een bakkerij.
column3: I used to work in a bakery.
column4: Tell a colleague about an earlier job. Use the simple past.
column5: Werkte is the simple past of werken: stem werk plus -te. The simple past suits a story or a former situation.

column2: Wij zijn gisteren naar Gent gereden.
column3: We drove to Ghent yesterday.
column4: Tell what happened on your trip yesterday. Use the perfect.
column5: Rijden with a destination uses zijn as the auxiliary: wij zijn gereden. The participle gereden closes the sentence.

column2: Zij woonde drie jaar in Brussel.
column3: She lived in Brussels for three years.
column4: Describe where a friend used to live. Use the simple past.
column5: Woonde is the simple past of wonen. The simple past describes a finished period.

column2: Ik heb vanochtend koffie gedronken.
column3: I drank coffee this morning.
column4: Report what you drank this morning. Use the perfect.
column5: The perfect reports what happened: heb plus the participle gedronken at the end. Vanochtend stays after the subject.

column2: Hij werkt nu bij een bank.
column3: He works at a bank now.
column4: Say where a colleague works today. Use the present.
column5: The present describes a situation that is true now. Nu marks that it is current.
